title: Server Software Component: Terminal Services DLL
shortTitle: Server Software Component: Terminal Services DLL
summary: Terminal Services DLL persistence abuses the service loader on Windows hosts that accept Remote Desktop connections. Services that run inside a shared generic host process are configured by a ServiceDll value in the Registry, which names the library the host loads on behalf of the service. For Terminal Services, now also called Remote Desktop Services, that value normally points to termsrv.dll in the system directory. An adversary who holds administrator rights can repoint the value to a library of their own, or patch the original file, so the code of the attacker runs whenever the service starts while normal remote desktop sessions continue to work. The same position allows feature abuse rather than code execution: modified libraries have historically enabled multiple concurrent sessions on editions that restrict them, and removed the prompts and session takeovers that normally warn a user who is logged in when someone else connects. Both variants leave configuration or file integrity evidence: Registry changes to the service parameters key and its ServiceDll value, file creation or modification events in the system directory, service start events that load a library outside the expected path, and library files whose signature, version, or hash differs from the vendor baseline.

beginner.definition: Remote Desktop lets you control a Windows computer over the network as if you were sitting in front of it. Windows loads a special program file to provide that service. This technique is about an attacker swapping or editing that file so their own code runs whenever the remote desktop service starts.
beginner.whyItMatters: Remote Desktop is one of the most common ways attackers keep a way back into a network, and this method makes that access automatic. Because the swap happens in a service setting, it survives restarts and looks like part of the operating system. A modified file can also unlock features the normal product blocks, such as several users connected at once. That lets an attacker work alongside a real user without being noticed and without triggering the usual warnings.
howItWorks: The attacker first gains administrator rights on the host, often through a stolen account.
They place their own program file somewhere on the disk and note its full path.
They change a Registry setting that tells the service which file to load at start-up.
When the remote desktop service starts, the host loads the attacker file and runs its code.
The service still works, so real users can connect exactly as they did before.
Sometimes the attacker edits the original file instead to unlock extra session features.
beginner.example: Imagine a hotel night desk where a card in the drawer tells the porter which master key to use. Someone replaces that card with one naming a copy of the key that also opens the staff flats. The porter keeps letting guests into their rooms as usual, and nobody notices the extra access until somebody reads the card.
takeaways: Watch Registry values that name service program files, not just the files themselves.
Check the signature, version and hash of the remote desktop service file.
Extra concurrent sessions or missing connection warnings can be a sign of tampering.

objectives: Explain how a Windows service is pointed at the program file it loads.
Describe how repointing or patching the terminal services library creates persistence.
Identify Registry and file integrity evidence of a swapped service library.
Recognise feature abuse such as forced or hidden remote desktop sessions.
Judge whether a service library change matches approved maintenance.
